This table has no placeholder 'unknown' row and no duplicate business keys, unlike most other similar tables. It is clean on both counts.

A generic process that creates placeholder rows is technically connected to this table, the same one used for OPERATOR_DIM. Unlike OPERATOR_DIM, where this process created a large share of the rows, here every row is a normal, fully approved record: this process has never actually run against this table.

This table was not part of a group of related tables retired in 2015-2016. Its schedule start date lines up with when it first went live, not with an older process being shut down. Caveat: the file used to check this carries its own warning that it may be incomplete, so this is not full proof the table was never affected by a similar retirement.

The placeholder-creation process file carries a leftover description referring to a different, unrelated table. This is a copy-paste artifact, not a sign that the wrong table is affected: the file's actual behavior confirms it targets AD_GRP_DIM.

Serious, same root cause: the step meant to correct a card's points earning flag also only compares against that same frozen 2020 staging table. For any card active since then, there is no working mechanism left in this table's process to ever fix that flag once it goes wrong

Confirmed: the final step into this table inserts new cards and updates existing ones by matching the internal key. Every update also overwrites the basket discount and points earning flags with whatever the staging table has, which, as found above, is empty from the true source. This is not a hypothesis anymore, it is confirmed in code: any card touched by today's process loses these two settings

Confirmed: the step that copies data from the raw feed into the next staging table always marks every card as approved, and computes a fingerprint used to detect what changed. That fingerprint is built from name, address and contact fields only. A card whose only change is to its discount or points settings would not be picked up as changed at all
26 other tables depend on this one, including the two largest transaction tables in the warehouse. This table has to be migrated before any of them

Two sources write this table. One is the running load, HQ, responsible for essentially the entire table and still active today. The other, labelled COST OVERRIDE, touched a small number of rows and has been frozen since May 2023, a one time manual correction rather than an ongoing process

items.text: The obvious staging tables for this data stopped being used in 2016. That does not mean this table itself went inactive: a separate, current process loads it directly from the store master system every day, most recently today.

The current process pulls data directly from 14 distinct tables joined in its own query. Re-checking all 14 against the Oracle catalog directly found that 3 of them are, in fact, real, queryable Oracle tables, not external HQ-side tables as first assumed: STORE_START_END_DATE (documented separately in this catalog), and SALES_AREA / SALES_AREA_ASSIGN (live, 313 and 929 rows, not in this project's scope). The other 11 (store_table, weis_store_status, weis_territory, weis_region, weis_store_hours, the synonym syn_hcd_loc_fuel_open_close, list_detail, lists, pos_areas, weis_county_code, weis_store_department_hours) were individually confirmed absent from every schema this discovery can query, so the true source system for those remains genuinely external and uninspected.

The current process's internal job logging is labeled under a different process's name, apparently copied from another table's loader and never updated. If job monitoring or alerting relies on that name, it is filed incorrectly.

Four columns on this table (legacy banner name, beer cafe open date, beer cafe close date, and pharmacy district number) are no longer updated by the current process. Their values are frozen history and will not change again unless a new process is built to maintain them. A fifth column, marketing cluster, is preserved as-is by the current process but is never assigned a new value.

The current process contains leftover logic for two specific stores that can never actually run, because those two stores are already excluded earlier in the same process. This is leftover code from an earlier version, not an active issue.

All 66 placeholder store records on this table were traced to a handful of supporting processes, most coming from one reusable utility that covers 9 different source tables. One of those processes has a misleading filename (it references a different table) but its own internal target confirms it is meant for this table; it has not actually created any records yet because no matching data exists so far.
